title: Asshole – rules
sub: The card game where the winner becomes king and the loser has to serve. Learn it in five minutes, play it all night.
goal: The goal: get rid of all your cards as fast as you can. Whoever is left holding cards at the end is the asshole – and has to hand their best cards to the king in the next round.

rules.setupLead: You need one ordinary pack of cards, no jokers, and 3 to 8 players. Four to six is the most fun. In Germany the game is usually played with a 32-card Skat pack.
rules.rankLead: The 7 is the lowest card, the ace the highest. Suits (♠♥♦♣) don't matter: a 9 of hearts is worth exactly as much as a 9 of spades.
rules.rankAlt: Order from low to high: 7, 8, 9, 10, jack, queen, king, ace.
rules.rankP: J = jack, Q = queen, K = king, A = ace. With 52 cards the 2 is the lowest, followed by 3, 4, 5, 6 and then as above.
rules.dealP: Shuffle and deal all cards one at a time, clockwise. If they don't divide evenly, some players get one card more – that's fine. Everyone sorts their hand and keeps it hidden.
rules.startP: In the very first round, whoever holds the 7 of clubs (with 52 cards: the 2 of clubs) starts by playing it (alone or with other 7s/2s). From the second round on, the asshole of the last round always starts.
rules.t1p: Whoever starts a trick plays a single card or several cards of the same rank face up in the middle, for example two 8s or three jacks.
rules.t2p: The next player clockwise has to play the same number of cards, but of a higher rank. On two 8s you can play two 10s or two kings, but not a single ace.
rules.t3p: You may always pass instead, even if you could beat it. Passing doesn't lock you out: next time it's your turn in the same trick, you can join in again.
rules.ckQ: Two 9s are on the table. What may you play?
rules.trickP: A trick goes round the table as often as needed. Once everyone else has passed in a row, the last cards played win it: the whole pile is put aside face down and is out of the game. The player who won it leads the next trick with anything they like.
rules.trickNote: Nobody beats Dana's two kings. She wins the trick and leads the next one.
rules.outP: As soon as you have played your last card, you are out and get the highest rank still free. The others keep playing without you. If nobody beats your last cards, the next player still in the game (clockwise) leads the new trick.
rules.ranksH: Ranks and the end of a round
rules.ranksLead: The order in which players run out of cards decides their rank for the next round:
rules.ranksP: With 4 players there is no citizen, with 3 players there is no vice king and no vice asshole: just king, citizen and asshole. The king is often called president instead.
rules.endP: The round is over as soon as only one player still has cards. That player is the asshole and doesn't need to play out the rest.
rules.gameP: As many rounds as you like – the real fun starts in round two, when the ranks come into play. If you'd like a winner, keep score: 2 points for the king, 1 for the vice king. The first to 10 points wins.
rules.swLead: Before every new round, the losers have to pay up. The asshole gives their best cards to the king and only gets the king's worst cards in return. That's why it is so hard to climb back up.
rules.swAlt: The asshole gives the ace of spades and the king of hearts to the king. The king gives back the 7 of diamonds and the 8 of clubs.
rules.s1p: The asshole shuffles and deals all the cards, as at the start.
rules.s2p: The asshole gives their 2 highest cards to the king, the vice asshole gives their 1 highest card to the vice king. No choice here: it has to be the highest ones.
rules.s3p: The king gives the asshole 2 cards back, the vice king gives 1 to the vice asshole. These may be any cards – usually the lowest ones.
rules.s4p: Citizens don't swap. The asshole leads the first trick, and the round runs as before.
rules.swWhy: With only 3 players, only the king and the asshole swap, 1 card each. Tip for the asshole: you lead first, so start with your lowest cards while everybody can still beat them.
rules.varLead: Hardly any card game has as many house rules as Asshole. Agree on them before you start. A few common ones:
rules.var1: 10 high: the 10 ranks between king and ace, so the order is 7, 8, 9, J, Q, K, 10, A. Popular in parts of Germany with the Skat pack.
rules.var2: 2 is the highest card: in the English-speaking world, with 52 cards, the order often runs 3 up to ace and then 2 as the top card.
rules.var3: Equal cards allowed: you may also play the same rank, for example a 9 on a 9. Some groups then skip the next player.
rules.var4: Out after passing: whoever passes sits out until the trick is over.
rules.var5: Bomb: four cards of the same rank win any trick at once, no matter what lies there.
rules.var6: Revolution: whoever plays four of a kind turns the order around for the rest of the round: the 7 (or 2 with 52 cards) is now the highest card, the ace the lowest.
rules.var7: No ace at the end: whoever goes out with an ace automatically becomes the asshole.
rules.var8: The king picks: instead of getting the highest cards, the king names a rank (“Do you have an ace?”). If the asshole has one, they have to hand it over.
rules.var9: New seats: after every round everyone sits down in order of rank. The king stays put, the vice king sits to their left, and so on until the asshole on the king's right.
rules.var10: With jokers: jokers beat every other card, sometimes they may also stand in for any rank.
rules.var11: Keep your aces: aces are protected during the card swap – the asshole keeps them and hands over their next-highest cards instead.
rules.faq1q: Can I play more cards than the player before me?
rules.faq1a: No. You always play exactly as many cards as were led. With three jacks on a pair you can still play two of them and keep the third.
rules.faq2q: Do I have to play if I can?
rules.faq2a: No, passing is always allowed. It is often clever to save high cards and pass instead.
rules.faq3q: I passed – can I play again in the same trick?
rules.faq3a: Yes, in the standard rules you can. Only in the variant Out after passing do you have to wait for the next trick.
rules.faq4q: Does the asshole have to give away aces and kings?
rules.faq4a: Yes, always the highest cards, even if it hurts. Some groups agree that aces are kept – see Variants.
rules.faq5q: How is Asshole different from President?
rules.faq5a: It's the same family of games. Asshole is the usual German name, often with 32 cards and the ace as the top card. President mostly uses 52 cards, often with the 2 as the highest card, and many more house rules.
rules.faq6q: What else is the game called?
rules.faq6a: Besides President it is known as Scum, Bum, Rich Man Poor Man or Trou du cul in France. Commercial versions include The Great Dalmuti.
rules.faq7q: How many players do I need?
rules.faq7a: At least 3, best 4 to 6. With more than 5 players, use a 52-card pack so that everyone gets enough cards.

strategy.h1: Become king – and stay on top
strategy.sub: The Asshole strategy guide. With only 32 cards, pairs and triples rule the table – knowing what to swap, when to pass and how to count aces makes all the difference.
strategy.principle: Asshole is all about tempo and control. In a 32-card Skat pack there are only eight ranks, so pairs and triples show up constantly. High cards buy you the lead – and the lead is how you dump low singletons before the endgame traps you.
strategy.swapH: Before the round: the card swap
strategy.swapLead: The asshole has no choice and must hand over their two highest cards. As king or vice king, picking what to send back is your most important move of the round.
strategy.giveH: What to give back to the asshole:
give: Loose low cards first (7, 8, 9). Unpaired low cards are the hardest to shed later because you need the lead to play them. Sending back a lone 7 and 9 cleans up your hand at once.
Keep your pairs intact. Never split a pair of 8s just to pass back a lower card. A low pair leaves in one lead – two mismatched single cards cost two separate turns.
Return two different ranks. Avoid handing back two cards of the same value. Giving the asshole a pair of 7s hands them a free combo they can drop on their very first lead.
Check the new cards first. Look at what the asshole gave you before choosing. If their king or ace completes a pair in your hand, protect that pair and trim loose low singletons instead.
As vice king (one card): Same rule – return your lowest unpaired card, not half of a pair.
strategy.notGive: What not to give back: a matching pair (like two 7s) or a high card that breaks up a strong set. Remember: the asshole leads the first trick, so gifting them a low pair lets them dump two cards immediately.
strategy.exAlt: Example swap. King's hand: a pair of 8s, a single 7, a single 9, a king and an ace. After the swap: you keep the pair of 8s, the king and the ace, and return the lone 7 and 9 to the asshole.
strategy.exWhy: Why? Instead of breaking the pair of 8s – or giving the asshole both 8s as a ready-made pair – you send back the unpaired 7 and 9. Your pair of 8s clears in one turn while the asshole is stuck with two loose low cards.
strategy.exVariant: 1-card swap (vice king): With one card to return, send back the lone 7 and keep the pair of 8s together.
strategy.exVariantAlt: 1-card swap: keep the pair of 8s and return the single 7

items: Use the asshole’s opening lead. From round two on, the asshole starts the first trick. Don’t lead a medium card you’ll need later – dump your lowest loose 7 or low pair straight away while everyone can still beat it.
Read your hand shape first. In a 32-card pack, almost every hand has pairs or triples. Decide early whether singles or pairs empty your hand faster and steer your leads toward that format.
Pass freely – passing costs nothing. In the basic rules you can pass and still jump back in later in the same trick. Let the others burn kings and aces against each other first.
Keep pairs and triples together. Breaking a pair of 10s just to beat a single 8 weakens your whole hand. Sets clear two or three cards in one go and are far harder to beat.
Playing from below: As asshole or vice asshole, don’t duel the king on trick one. Slip your middle cards into cheap tricks and wait for the top ranks to spend their aces.

Count the aces and kings. With only 32 cards it is easy to track all four aces and four kings. Once the fourth ace drops, any king guarantees the lead; once the kings are gone, a queen rules the table.
Watch high pairs closely. Halfway through a 32-card round, even a pair of jacks or queens frequently wins the trick outright because the higher ranks have already been split.
Break the leader’s rhythm. If the king keeps leading pairs and winning them back, invest a strong pair once to steal the lead – then switch to singles or triples.
Save your ace for a real payoff. Don’t burn an ace on a single 9 if you have no low junk to dump next. An ace is worth most when winning the lead clears weak cards or sets up your finish.
Track everyone’s card count. When someone is down to two or three cards, check whether they’ve been winning with singles or pairs and lead the opposite format.

Plan your last two turns together. Before taking the lead with an ace or king, know how you’ll go out. Cleanest finish: win the trick with your highest card, then drop your final pair or lone low card.

Go out on your weakest card. Holding an ace and a lone 7? Take the lead with the ace and finish on the 7 – nobody can stop your last lead. Leaving the 7 for last only hurts if you lose the lead first.
Keep a pair as your closer. Finishing with a pair clears two cards in one turn and stops you from getting stuck with a single 7 or 8.
Fight for every rank. Even if the king is already out, second place (vice king) earns you a top card next round instead of handing one over – and staying out of asshole always matters.
Watch your house rules. Playing with “No ace at the end” or “10 high”? Make sure your top card wins the second-to-last trick and never ends up as your final play.

strategy.cardsLead: In the basic 32-card game no card has a special power, yet a few ranks and sets decide almost every round.

cards.p: The highest card in the pack. On singles, an ace cannot be beaten and hands you the next lead.
items: Save it for the moment you need to dump low singletons or close out the round.
Holding two aces? A pair of aces beats any pair – only split them if a single ace wins the round.
With the house rule “No ace at the end”, win the second-to-last trick with your ace so you never go out on it.

cards.p: Second-highest rank, and unbeatable as soon as all four aces are out. Use single kings to draw out opponents’ aces, or hold a pair of kings to dominate pair tricks.

cards.h: Pairs – The heart of a 32-card game
cards.p: With only eight ranks in the pack, pairs appear constantly. Even a low pair clears two cards in one turn, while a pair of queens or kings often wins the trick outright.

cards.h: Three of a kind – Trick killers
cards.p: In a 32-card pack, triples are almost impossible to beat – even three 9s frequently clear the table and return the lead straight to you. Avoid splitting a triple unless you have no other choice.
In round one the 7 of clubs opens the game – drop all your 7s together if you can. On every later round, use early leads to shed single 7s and 8s before the endgame starts.
Clears four cards at once and can only be beaten by a higher four. Playing with the Bomb or Revolution variant? Hold your four of a kind until flipping the order lets your 7s and 8s run the table.

mistakes: Handing the asshole a pair in the swap. Returning two 7s instead of a 7 and a 9 gives the asshole a free pair to dump on their opening lead.
Breaking pairs for cheap tricks. Splitting a pair of 10s just to beat a single 8 leaves you with a loose singleton and throws away a strong pair.
Burning aces too early. Spending an ace on trick one without a plan leaves you defenseless in the endgame.
Never passing. Passing is free in the standard rules – let other players exhaust their kings and aces on each other first.
Not counting aces and kings. In a 32-card pack there are only eight top cards total. Tracking them tells you the exact moment your king or queen becomes unbeatable.
Getting stranded with a lone 7 at the end. Playing high cards first and leaving a single 7 for last traps you on the sidelines – clear low cards while you can still win the lead.

quick.rule: Lead 1–4 equal cards. Next player beats with the same count and a higher rank – or passes anytime. Last player standing wins the trick and leads next.
quick.rankNote: Suits don’t matter (with 52 cards: 2 to ace). Round 1 starts with 7♣ (or 2♣); after that the asshole leads.
quick.swap1: King ↔ Asshole: Asshole deals, gives 2 highest, gets any 2 back – and leads first.
quick.swap2: Vice king ↔ Vice asshole: Vice asshole gives 1 highest; vice king returns any 1.
quick.swap3: Citizens: everyone in the middle – no swap.
